title: Demographic and Growth Dynamics Jointly Shape Grassland Productivity Under Extreme Drought
content:
Despite intensifying droughts threatening grassland productivity, few studies have explicitly clarified the respective roles of demographic (plant density) and growth-related (individual size) processes, which are critical for predicting its changes. By separating their contributions, we uncovered their trade-off in driving drought-induced productivity changes, mediated by leaf traits. These dynamics were further modulated by strategies of plant functional groups, with graminoids prioritizing survival and forbs allocating more resources to individual growth. This work reveals how demographic and growth dynamics jointly shape grassland productivity over time, advancing mechanistic understanding of ecosystem adaptation to drought.


ABSTRACT

Understanding how plant communities maintain productivity in arid environments remains a key ecological question. Using two independent 4-year drought experiments with a 66% reduction in growing season precipitation in a semi-arid grassland, we found that reductions in plant density and individual size jointly contributed to drought-induced declines in aboveground net primary productivity (ANPP), and that their relative importance depends on drought duration, intensity, and plant functional group. For graminoids, ANPP decline was primarily driven by reduced individual size, whereas for forbs it was driven by reduced plant density. There was a trade-off between the contributions of plant density and individual size to productivity, which was mediated by leaf functional traits, including leaf carbon content and leaf nitrogen. Our findings highlight the role of the trade-off between demographic and growth-related processes in regulating productivity under climate change.
